title: A comprehensive atlas of the bonobo gut bacteriome and its associated host and exposome factors.
ehr_evidence: In the zoo setting, data were collected using observations, historical records retrieved from the studbook or from the Zoological Information Management System (ZIMS), questionnaires and diet sheets filled in by zoo staff.
summary: A standardized microbiome atlas study of 644 fecal 16S samples from 212 wild and zoo-housed bonobos (Pan paniscus) examining how host and exposome factors shape gut bacteriome composition.
key_findings: Gut bacterial beta diversity was significantly associated with captive vs. wild lifestyle (PERMANOVA: R2 = 28.7%, p < 0.001)
Alpha diversity (inverse Simpson) was higher in wild than zoo-housed bonobos (LMM: β = 0.935 ± 0.311 SE, p = 0.020)
Grooming bond strength was the strongest predictor of gut bacteriome similarity (posterior mean = 1.055, 95% CI: [0.496, 1.609]), exceeding genetic relatedness
Antibiotic use was associated with lower similarity to the wild phenotype (posterior mean = −0.298, 95% CI: [−0.407, −0.189])
Diets high in fiber, starch, and browse were associated with more wild-like gut bacteriomes (fiber posterior mean = 0.167, 95% CI: [0.056, 0.281])
captured_features: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (V4 region) ASV counts and taxa tables
Host factors (age, sex, reproductive state, rearing history)
Exposome factors (diet, antibiotic/medicine use, Bristol stool score, seasonality, outdoor access)
Social behavior (grooming bond strength, proximity bond strength, tenure, dominance rank)
study_design: Cross-sectional microbiome atlas with dyadic analyses (zoo-housed and wild cohorts)
population: 212 wild and zoo-housed bonobos (Pan paniscus), ages 1.1–70.6 years, from 11 European zoos and two wild communities (Bompusa East and West) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
exposure_domain: exposome factors including diet, antibiotic/medicine use, social contact, early-life adversity, and environment
limitations: 16S rRNA sequencing does not provide strain-level resolution, limiting transmission inference
Assumes the studied wild bonobo populations have a native, non-dysbiotic bacteriome
Only two wild communities were sampled, limiting generalizability of native microbiome variability
data_availability_statement: Sequencing data have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive under project ENA: PRJEB86099 and are publicly available as of the date of publication. Pseudonymized sample data have been deposited and are publicly available as of the date of publication at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14913431. Table 1 includes sample (meta)data on pseudonymized group and individual identity, sampling date, sequencing plate, DNA extraction method, and all associated data analyzed within the current study. Data on the dyadic level are found in tables 2 and 3, an ASV-level count table per sample in table 4, and an ASV-level taxa annotation in table 5. All original code has been deposited and is publicly available as of the date of publication at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14911049. Any additional information required to reanalyze the data reported in this paper is available from the lead contact upon request.
